slot.title: Check: Yggdrasil and the Nine Worlds
slot.lessonGoal: Recall how Norse sources picture Yggdrasil connecting the Nine Worlds.
objectives: Describe Yggdrasil as the world tree at the centre of Norse cosmology
Name the realms of gods, humans, and the dead among the Nine Worlds

items.prompt: What is Yggdrasil in Norse cosmology?

options.text: A vast ash tree that stands at the centre of the universe
A rainbow bridge that connects the realm of the gods to the human world
A fortress-wall made from the eyelashes of a giant
A primordial realm of fire and heat

explanations.brief: Yggdrasil is a vast ash tree at the centre of the universe.
explanations.standard: According to the Poetic Edda and Prose Edda, Yggdrasil is a great ash tree that stands at the centre of the cosmos, with branches covering the world.
explanations.detailed: The lesson describes Yggdrasil as an ash tree at the heart of the Nine Worlds. “A rainbow bridge that connects the realm of the gods to the human world” describes Bifrost, the rainbow bridge. “A fortress-wall made from the eyelashes of a giant” refers to Midgard's creation. “A primordial realm of fire and heat” is Muspelheim.

items.prompt: Which world is the realm of human beings?

explanations.brief: Midgard is the world of humans.
explanations.standard: The lesson states Midgard is the world of human beings, created as a fortress from Ymir's eyelashes.
explanations.detailed: Midgard is the human world. “Asgard” is the realm of the Æsir gods. “Hel” is the abode of the dead. “Jotunheim” is the land of giants.

items.prompt: Which realm is described as the abode of the dead who died of illness or old age?

explanations.brief: Hel is the realm of the dead who died of sickness or old age.
explanations.standard: Hel is the dark realm that receives those who died of illness or old age, and is the most populous afterlife destination.
explanations.detailed: Hel is explicitly the abode of those who died of illness or old age. “Niflheim” is primordial ice and mist, not the dead's realm. “Muspelheim” is fire. “Svartalfheim” is the realm of dwarves.

items.prompt: Which world is the home of the Æsir gods?

explanations.brief: Asgard is the realm of the Æsir gods.
explanations.standard: The lesson says Asgard is the realm of the Æsir gods, connected to Midgard by the rainbow bridge Bifrost.
explanations.detailed: Asgard is home to the Æsir. “Vanaheim” is the realm of the Vanir, another group of deities, not the Æsir. “Alfheim” is the elf realm. “Midgard” is the human world.

items.prompt: Why do the descriptions of Yggdrasil's roots differ between the Poetic Edda and the Prose Edda?

options.text: The Poetic Edda was written after the Prose Edda and corrected its mistakes.
Norse cosmology had no fixed scripture, and later writers rearranged older material.
The Prose Edda describes a different tree altogether, not Yggdrasil.
The roots changed over time due to natural growth, so later sources record later stages.

explanations.brief: Differences stem from the lack of fixed scripture and Snorri's rearrangement of older material.
explanations.standard: Norse cosmology was transmitted orally with no written scripture, so details remained fluid. Snorri Sturluson, compiling the Prose Edda, systematised and reinterpreted older traditions, causing the root accounts to differ from those in the Poetic Edda.
explanations.detailed: Oral transmission without fixed scripture meant details could vary. Snorri rearranged and systematised material, leading to a different root arrangement. “The Poetic Edda was written after the Prose Edda and corrected its mistakes.” is false: the Poetic Edda is earlier. “The Prose Edda describes a different tree altogether, not Yggdrasil.” is not supported by the lesson; the Prose Edda also describes Yggdrasil. “The roots changed over time due to natural growth, so later sources record later stages.” is not mentioned in the lesson, which attributes differences to transmission, not physical change.
